title: Registration and device-enrollment data can identify the homeowner
description: The flow carries account-registration details and device-enrollment metadata from the homeowner to the Home Hub. Names, email/phone, account identifiers, home address, device serial numbers, MAC addresses, and sensor/camera inventory can directly identify or single out the homeowner or household when processed by the Home Hub.
assumptions: Assumes the registration/enrollment payload includes personal account data and unique device identifiers tied to a household.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only confirms applicability of Identifiability to ExternalEntity->Process flows, not the detailed subtree.

title: Enrollment metadata may link the homeowner across devices and services
description: Unique device identifiers and account identifiers submitted during enrollment can allow the Home Hub, or parties receiving the data later, to link multiple cameras/sensors and repeated interactions to the same homeowner or household, building a consolidated profile of the home environment.
assumptions: Assumes device serial numbers, MAC addresses, account IDs, or similar stable identifiers are transmitted or derived during enrollment.
uncertainty_note: Detailed threat-tree node chosen by best judgement; retrieved context establishes Linkability as applicable for this flow type but does not provide subtree detail.

title: Registration and enrollment reveal sensitive household information
description: The data flow can disclose privacy-sensitive information to the Home Hub, such as the existence and number of cameras/sensors, device locations or roles, occupancy-related setup choices, and contact details. This reveals characteristics of the household and its monitoring setup beyond what may be strictly necessary for basic operation.
assumptions: Assumes enrollment includes device type, placement/role, and account/contact information.
uncertainty_note: Threat applies to disclosure at the receiving process; exact subtree id is approximate due to limited retrieved subtree context.

title: Homeowner may be unable to prove or contest enrollment actions
description: If the Home Hub does not provide privacy-preserving evidence of consent and enrollment actions, the homeowner may later be unable to demonstrate what account-registration details were submitted, which devices were enrolled, or whether enrollment occurred with their authorization. This can undermine accountability for privacy-relevant setup actions.
assumptions: Assumes the system lacks reliable, user-accessible records or receipts for registration and device-enrollment events.
uncertainty_note: Repudiation-related subtree id is selected by best judgement; applicability is genuine but exact node naming may vary across LINDDUN Pro materials.

title: Homeowner may be unaware of what personal and device data enrollment collects
description: During account registration and device enrollment, the homeowner may not understand which personal details, device identifiers, and household characteristics are collected by the Home Hub, for what purposes, and with whom they may later be shared. This creates a privacy threat through insufficient transparency at the point of collection.
assumptions: Assumes the registration/enrollment interface does not clearly explain collection, purposes, retention, or downstream sharing.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree id is approximate; retrieved context supports Unawareness for this flow type but not the detailed node.

title: Registration and enrollment may collect more data than necessary or without valid consent
description: The Home Hub may request or ingest excessive personal data or device metadata during account creation and enrollment, or proceed without a valid legal basis, granular consent, or purpose limitation. Examples include collecting unnecessary contact details, precise device identifiers, or detailed household inventory not required for setup.
assumptions: Assumes at least some registration/enrollment fields are optional or not strictly necessary for core provisioning, or that consent/legal-basis handling may be weak.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance is grounded in common data-minimization/consent concerns for onboarding flows; exact subtree id is approximate.

title: Temporary access code can identify or single out a guest user
description: The temporary access code submitted by the guest may act as a unique or near-unique identifier for a specific guest visit, reservation, or household invitation. If the Home Hub logs or otherwise associates the code with a person, time, or stay, the flow enables identification of the guest.
assumptions: Assumes the temporary code is unique per guest, booking, or visit and is processed or logged by the Home Hub.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only provided applicable threat types, not detailed node ids.

title: Guest code submission may be provable and later used against the guest
description: If the Home Hub records the entered temporary access code together with timestamps or device context, it may create evidence that a particular guest attempted or performed an unlock action. This can reduce the guest's plausible deniability regarding presence at the property or participation in the access event.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub stores audit logs or event records linking code entry to a guest, booking, or time window.
uncertainty_note: Detailed LINDDUN Pro node id is approximate; applicability depends on whether the system keeps attributable logs.

title: Observation of code-entry interaction can reveal guest participation
description: An observer who can monitor the communication or visible interaction between the guest and the Home Hub may infer that a guest is currently present and attempting entry, even without learning the code itself. The mere existence and timing of this flow can reveal involvement in the system.
assumptions: Assumes an attacker can observe the communication channel, keypad interaction, or system responses around code entry.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; grounded in LINDDUN detecting via observed communication/system responses.

title: Entered temporary access code may disclose sensitive personal or behavioral information
description: The temporary access code and its associated metadata can disclose information such as which guest booking is active, expected arrival window, occupancy status, or that a specific invited person is authorized to enter. If exposed beyond what is necessary, this flow can reveal personal information about the guest or household.
assumptions: Assumes the code is linked in backend logic or logs to a guest identity, reservation, or access schedule.
uncertainty_note: Detailed node id is approximate because the retrieved context did not include the Dd subtree.

title: Guest may be unaware how code-entry data is processed or retained
description: When entering a temporary access code, the guest may not understand what personal data the Home Hub collects, whether the code entry is logged, how long records are retained, or with whom access-event data is shared. This creates a privacy threat from insufficient transparency.

title: Processing of guest access-code data may occur without valid consent or another proper legal basis
description: The Home Hub processes the guest's temporary access code and related access-event data to authenticate entry. If the guest has not been properly informed or has not provided valid consent where required, or if another lawful basis is not established, this flow may constitute non-compliant processing of personal data.

title: Linkability of household activity patterns through repeated event records
description: The local event log stores repeated motion, door, and sensor events over time. Even if individual entries seem innocuous, their timestamps and device identifiers can be linked to reconstruct routines such as occupancy, sleep/wake cycles, and arrivals/departures.
assumptions: Assumes the log retains per-event timestamps and stable sensor or device identifiers across entries.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only provided applicability by threat type, not detailed threat-tree nodes.

title: Identifiability of residents from logged sensor events
description: Event sequences written to the local log may make specific residents identifiable by their distinctive movement patterns, room usage, or door-opening habits, especially in single-occupant homes or where events can be correlated with known schedules.
assumptions: Assumes event records include enough temporal or location detail to distinguish individuals or households.
uncertainty_note: Detailed threat-tree node citation is approximate; applicability is inferred from standard LINDDUN identifiability reasoning for event logs.

title: Disclosure of sensitive in-home behavior via local event logging
description: Writing raw motion, door, and sensor events to the local event log creates a repository of sensitive behavioral data. Unauthorized access to the datastore could reveal presence at home, room usage, daily routines, absences, and potentially special-category inferences such as health or religious practices.
assumptions: Assumes the local event log can be accessed by local administrators, malware, other components, or physical attackers if not adequately protected.
uncertainty_note: Threat clearly applies, but the exact tree node id is approximate due to missing detailed node mapping in the retrieved context.

title: Unawareness of ongoing behavioral logging in the home
description: Residents and visitors may be unaware that the Home Hub persistently writes motion, door, and sensor events to a local log, what granularity is stored, and how long the records are retained. This undermines transparency about monitoring inside the home.
assumptions: Assumes the system does not provide clear in-context notice or accessible explanations about local event logging.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; the threat is grounded in lack of transparency around logging rather than a specific cited subtree.

title: Logging may exceed necessity or retention expectations
description: Persistently storing detailed motion, door, and sensor events in the local event log may be unnecessary for the stated purpose if only short-term state or aggregated summaries are needed. Excessive granularity or retention would conflict with data minimization and storage limitation expectations.
assumptions: Assumes some logged fields, precision, or retention period are broader than strictly required for functionality, diagnostics, or security.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on actual purpose, retention policy, and legal basis, which are not provided.

title: Residents cannot plausibly deny inferred activities recorded in the log
description: The local event log may be treated as authoritative evidence of household movements or door usage. If entries are retained and attributable to a home or person, occupants may be unable to repudiate conclusions drawn from the records, even though sensor events can be ambiguous or context-dependent.
assumptions: Assumes the log is used for audit, dispute resolution, or later review and is considered trustworthy by operators or third parties.
uncertainty_note: This is a weaker threat for this flow and depends on downstream use of the log; included with moderate uncertainty.

title: Uploaded clips can be linked to a specific household or resident account
description: When the Home Hub uploads recorded camera clips to cloud storage, the clips are typically accompanied by stable identifiers such as device ID, account ID, household ID, timestamps, and camera metadata. This enables the cloud service to link multiple uploads over time to the same home and potentially to specific residents, creating a longitudinal view of behavior and occupancy.
assumptions: Assumes uploads include persistent identifiers or metadata needed to associate clips with the correct cloud account/device.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only confirms applicability of L to Process->DataStore flows, not the detailed subtree.

title: Video clips reveal highly identifying household and behavioral information
description: Recorded camera clips uploaded from the Home Hub may contain faces, voices, interiors, visitors, routines, and precise timestamps. Even if the clip payload is the primary data, associated metadata can further identify the household and infer sensitive patterns such as presence at home, sleep/work schedules, or social relationships.
assumptions: Assumes the uploaded clips contain personal data and are not irreversibly anonymized before upload.
uncertainty_note: Detailed tree node id is approximate; the context supports Identifiability on this flow type but does not provide the exact subtree.

title: Cloud storage enables broad disclosure of intimate in-home footage
description: Once clips are uploaded to Cloud Video Storage, the datastore becomes a concentration point for sensitive in-home video. Unauthorized internal access, external compromise, misconfiguration, or overly broad sharing features could disclose footage and metadata to parties beyond the expected recipients.
assumptions: Assumes cloud-stored clips are accessible by service components, administrators, integrations, or sharing mechanisms beyond the Home Hub itself.
uncertainty_note: Threat is clearly applicable to the datastore receiving the flow; exact subtree id is best-effort.

title: Stored clips permit detection of occupancy and routine patterns
description: Accumulated uploaded clips and their timestamps allow the cloud datastore to reveal when residents are home, away, asleep, receiving visitors, or following recurring routines. Even without watching every clip, metadata such as motion-trigger times, upload frequency, and camera location can expose private activities and habits.
assumptions: Assumes the cloud retains timestamps, event metadata, or clip organization over time.
uncertainty_note: Exact Dd subtree id is approximate; applicability of Detectability to Process->DataStore interactions is supported by the mapping context.

title: Residents or bystanders may be unaware that footage is uploaded to the cloud
description: The Home Hub's upload of recorded clips to cloud storage may not be sufficiently visible to residents, guests, or passers-by captured by the camera. If cloud upload is automatic or enabled by default, affected individuals may not understand that footage leaves the local environment and is retained remotely.
assumptions: Assumes cloud upload is automatic, backgrounded, or not clearly signaled at the time of recording/upload.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-effort because the retrieved context does not include detailed Unawareness subtree mappings.

title: Cloud retention and secondary use of uploaded clips may exceed user expectations or legal basis
description: Uploading recorded clips to cloud storage can create non-compliance risks if retention periods are excessive, purposes are expanded beyond home security, cross-border transfers occur without safeguards, or rights such as access/deletion are not properly supported for the stored footage.
assumptions: Assumes the cloud service determines retention, processing purposes, or storage location for uploaded clips.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance is plausible for this datastore, but exact legal obligations depend on jurisdiction, controller/processor roles, and service design.

title: Real-time motion alert may disclose excessive occupancy/activity information to another service
description: The Home Hub forwards a real-time motion alert to the mobile app backend. Motion alerts are personal data because they reveal presence, behavior patterns, and occupancy of a household. This flow creates a data-disclosure risk if the alert contains more detail than strictly necessary for backend processing or if the backend is not strictly limited to the intended receiving party and purpose. Examples include sending precise timestamps, room/device identifiers, continuous event streams, or rich metadata when a minimal event signal would suffice.
assumptions: Assumes the motion alert relates to an identifiable household, user account, device, or location, and that the backend is a distinct receiving party/process across a trust or exposure boundary.

title: Motion-alert payload may enable linkage of household activity across events and services
description: If the Home Hub includes stable identifiers such as hub ID, household ID, sensor ID, account ID, or persistent pseudonyms in each motion alert, the backend can link multiple alerts over time and correlate them with other datasets. This may allow reconstruction of routines, occupancy schedules, and behavior patterns beyond the immediate alerting purpose.
assumptions: Assumes stable identifiers or sufficiently unique metadata are present in the flow and can be correlated by the backend.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is based on general LINDDUN linkage categories; exact node id may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Real-time motion alerts may allow identification of a specific household or resident
description: Even if the alert does not contain an explicit name, combinations of device identifiers, address-linked hub identifiers, account references, or distinctive timing/location metadata may allow the backend to identify the data subject or household. Identification risk increases when the backend already holds subscriber, device-registration, or address information.
assumptions: Assumes the backend can associate the incoming alert with customer/account/device records.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is based on general LINDDUN identifiability categories; exact node id may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Motion alerts reveal detectability of user presence and in-home activity
description: The mere transmission of a real-time motion alert makes the occurrence of in-home activity detectable to the backend. Even without full identification, the backend can observe that some monitored environment has become active at a specific time, which may expose sensitive occupancy patterns such as when residents are home, asleep, or away.
assumptions: Assumes the backend can observe event timing and source context for the alert.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is based on general LINDDUN detectability categories; exact node id may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Backend-side secondary use of motion alerts may exceed user expectations
description: Once received by the mobile app backend, real-time motion alerts could be used for purposes beyond immediate notification delivery, such as analytics, profiling, feature experimentation, or sharing with affiliated services. Such use may be unexpected or insufficiently transparent to users, creating an unawareness threat regarding how intimate in-home activity data is processed.
assumptions: Assumes users may not be clearly informed that backend processing includes retention, analytics, or secondary uses beyond delivering the alert.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is based on general LINDDUN unawareness categories; exact node id may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Backend processing of motion alerts may be non-compliant if not necessary, proportionate, or properly governed
description: Processing real-time motion alerts at the mobile app backend may violate privacy obligations if the transfer lacks a valid legal basis, exceeds data-minimization limits, retains data longer than necessary, or is not covered by appropriate transparency, purpose limitation, and processor/controller arrangements. Because motion data can reveal intimate household behavior, compliance requirements are likely stringent.
assumptions: Assumes applicable privacy regulation or internal policy imposes requirements on lawful basis, minimization, retention, transparency, and access governance for household activity data.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is based on general LINDDUN non-compliance categories; exact node id may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Notification content can link the event to a specific household or resident
description: A motion-detected push notification sent from the backend to the homeowner can act as a persistent identifier or linkage point when it contains device names, address labels, account identifiers, or stable notification tokens. Observers of the message stream or platform intermediaries may link repeated alerts to the same home and infer occupancy patterns.
assumptions: Assumes notification payload or metadata includes stable identifiers, device labels, or account-linked routing information.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgement; retrieved context confirms L applies to Process->ExternalEntity flows but does not provide finer-grained node ids.

title: Push notification reveals sensitive motion-event information to unintended parties
description: The backend may disclose personal information through the notification content or metadata, such as that motion was detected at a particular home and time. This may be exposed to push-service providers, lock-screen viewers, shared devices, or anyone with access to the phone, revealing presence-at-home patterns and security-relevant events.
assumptions: Assumes notification content is visible on lock screen or accessible to intermediaries, and includes event details beyond a generic alert.
uncertainty_note: Specific node id is approximate; disclosure risk clearly applies to this flow.

title: Lack of evidence about notification delivery or viewing can create repudiation disputes
description: If the backend does not keep reliable records of notification generation, dispatch, delivery status, or user acknowledgement, either party may later dispute whether the homeowner was informed about the motion event. This undermines accountability around privacy-relevant alerts and user expectations.
assumptions: Assumes the system relies on notifications for informing users about surveillance events and lacks auditable delivery/receipt records.
uncertainty_note: Repudiation applicability is plausible for this flow, but depends on whether delivery/audit evidence is in scope.

title: Notification content may enable inference of occupancy and daily routines
description: Even if the notification contains limited text, repeated motion-detected alerts over time allow the recipient, intermediaries, or anyone observing the device to infer when people are home, away, asleep, or active. This derives sensitive behavioral patterns from the event stream.
assumptions: Assumes alerts are sent with timestamps/frequency sufficient to reveal patterns.
uncertainty_note: Specific node id is approximate; derivation threat is strongly grounded in the repeated event nature of this flow.

title: Notification may omit necessary context about why data is processed and shared
description: A motion alert pushed to the homeowner may not provide enough information about what triggered it, what data was processed, whether images/video are involved, who else may receive the event, or how long related data is retained. This limits the homeowner's ability to understand the privacy implications of the event processing.

title: Homeowner may be unaware that motion events are being pushed via third-party notification infrastructure
description: If the backend uses platform push services, the homeowner may not realize that event metadata is transmitted through external providers or displayed on lock screens. This creates insufficient awareness of how surveillance-related data leaves the backend and reaches the device.

This can violate user choices and applicable privacy requirements.

title: Shared aggregated analytics may still reveal sensitive inferences
